lines: - "⛔ THE MIGRATION IS A SEPARATE ONE-SHOT CONTAINER AND NOTHING ELSE RUNS IT. The server does NOT migrate at boot. Upstream builds docker/migration/Dockerfile from the server image just to run, from /app/packages/server, node dist/cli.js system:migrate:latest followed by node dist/cli.js tenants:migrate:latest (both command names confirmed in modules/CLI/commands; those are nest-commander SUBCOMMAND names that happen to end in the word latest, not image tags, so do not 'fix' them). Do not build that image: add a one-shot service using the PINNED server image with working_dir /app/packages/server and those two commands, restart: 'no', and give it the same DB_* and SYSTEM_DB_* environment as the server. It has no wait-for-it, so wrap it in a bounded retry (roughly: for i in 1..30, try the system migrate, sleep 5 on failure) rather than depending on depends_on, which only waits for the container to start and not for MariaDB to accept connections. Verify it with the script in the body of this file, which checks the system database has tables AND that the check itself ran."

- "DATABASE WIRING, AND THE VARIABLE NAME REALLY IS MISSPELLED. The server reads DB_HOST, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD, DB_CHARSET, SYSTEM_DB_NAME and TENANT_DB_NAME_PERFIX. That is PERFIX, not PREFIX, in tenant-database.ts:10; spell it correctly and it silently falls back to the built-in default prefix. SYSTEM_DB_* and TENANT_DB_* each fall back to the matching DB_* (system-database.ts:3-8, tenant-database.ts:3-8), so with one MariaDB you only need the DB_* trio plus SYSTEM_DB_NAME. DB_HOST is the compose service name of the MariaDB container, not localhost. There is no DATABASE_URL in this app, so redu's injected PG* variables are irrelevant here: there is no managed database to inject them from."

lines: - "⛔⛔⛔ THE SESSION SIGNING KEY IS APP_JWT_SECRET, NOT JWT_SECRET, AND UPSTREAM'S OWN PRODUCTION COMPOSE SETS THE WRONG ONE. packages/server/src/common/config/jwt.ts:4 is process.env.APP_JWT_SECRET with a fallback to a six-character constant that is printed in .env.example, and Auth.module.ts:58-64 hands that value to JwtModule for both signing and verification (HS384). docker-compose.prod.yml:71 passes JWT_SECRET, which no code reads. So a by-the-book upstream deploy signs every session token with a publicly documented constant, and anyone who knows it can mint a valid token for any user on your instance. SET APP_JWT_SECRET to a long random value, and REUSE THE SAME VALUE ON EVERY REDEPLOY: change it and every issued token stops validating and everybody is logged out. Prove it after boot in BOTH directions, because an absence proves nothing: run `sudo docker exec bigcapital-server sh -c 'printenv APP_JWT_SECRET | wc -c'` and confirm the length is far above 7 (this is also what tells you the exec worked at all), then confirm the container is the one serving traffic with `sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Image}}'`. Setting JWT_SECRET as well is harmless and does nothing."

- "⛔⛔ BIGCAPITAL CREATES A NEW DATABASE PER ORGANIZATION AT RUNTIME, SO A redu MANAGED DATABASE CANNOT HOST IT, AND THAT IS WHY THE DATABASE IS IN THE COMPOSE. modules/TenantDBManager/TenantDBManager.ts:60-66 issues CREATE DATABASE <prefix><organizationId> on the SYSTEM connection every time an organization is built (BuildOrganization.service.ts:59-62), and TenantDBManager.ts:86 drops it again. Upstream makes that work with one line in docker/mariadb/init.sql: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* to the app user WITH GRANT OPTION. redu's managed MySQL and MariaDB grant ALL PRIVILEGES on ONE database only, and the superuser flag that managed Postgres honours is not implemented for those engines, so the CREATE DATABASE is refused and the failure lands AFTER the account already exists: you get a user who can sign in and an organization that never finishes building. Managed Postgres is not an alternative either, because system-database.ts:5 and tenant-database.ts:5 both hardcode client: mysql. WHAT THIS FORCES, say it to the user before they approve the plan: your books live on the app VM's own disk, on a docker volume, with no managed database beside them. Nothing else on redu backs that volume up for you, delete_deployment destroys it, and a mysqldump on a schedule is now YOUR job. If you would rather have a managed MariaDB, the only way is to add GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* by hand on the managed DB VM: that works, it costs another GBP 0.0174/hr, and it is NOT durable, because a DB VM rebuild loses the grant and the next organization someone creates fails."

- "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: NOBODY, UNLESS YOU CLOSE SIGNUP AT DEPLOY TIME. There is no instance-wide admin account and no install wizard. Every signup creates its OWN organization and owns it (AuthSignup.service.ts:66 calls createTenant for each one), and building that organization creates another MySQL database on your VM. Registration is OPEN by default: signup-restrictions.ts:6 defaults SIGNUP_DISABLED to false, and AuthSignup.service.ts:111-112 returns early from the restriction check when it is false, which means SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS and SIGNUP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS are COMPLETELY INERT on their own. The safe-by-construction pattern, and it is a real one here: set SIGNUP_DISABLED=true AND SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS to the operator's own address BEFORE the hostname exists. Only that address can then register, and the first account it creates owns the first organization. Leave the default in place on a public hostname and any stranger can create an account, an organization and a database on your VM, and you are paying for the disk."

-  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH, verified in Auth.controller.ts:34-37 where @PublicRoute() sits on the whole /auth controller: POST /api/auth/signin, POST /api/auth/signup, POST /api/auth/signup/verify, POST /api/auth/send_reset_password, POST /api/auth/reset_password/:token and GET /api/auth/meta. Everything else is behind the global JWT guard. GET /api/auth/meta returns {signupDisabled: <bool>} and is the endpoint the verification script in the body of this file uses, along with an actual refused signup, because a flag reporting the right value is not proof the behaviour changed."

The refusal itself answers 400 with type SIGNUP_RESTRICTED_NOT_ALLOWED, which is how you tell the restriction fired rather than ordinary body validation."

- "PIN EVERY IMAGE. Upstream's docker-compose.prod.yml uses the rolling tag for bigcapitalhq/webapp and bigcapitalhq/server, a rolling v1.30 tag for envoyproxy/envoy and the bare major 7 for gotenberg/gotenberg. Registry-checked on 2026-08-17: server and webapp both publish v0.25.31, pushed the same day; the rolling envoy v1.30 tag and v1.30.11 return the SAME manifest digest, and the gotenberg major 7 tag and 7.10.2 likewise, so pinning loses nothing at all. Use bigcapitalhq/server:v0.25.31, bigcapitalhq/webapp:v0.25.31, envoyproxy/envoy:v1.30.11 and gotenberg/gotenberg:7.10.2. Keep gotenberg on the 7 line: that is the major version Bigcapital targets and 8 is a different API. Never write a rolling tag into this stack; server and webapp must move together or the SPA calls endpoints the server does not have."

- "THE DATA SERVICES ARE FORWARD SUBSTITUTIONS AND YOU SHOULD KNOW WHICH LINES ARE OURS. Upstream BUILDS its own mariadb image FROM mariadb:10.2 (EOL 2022) and its own redis FROM redis:6.2.21. This recipe replaces both with official images, mariadb:11.4.12 and redis:7.4.10-alpine, which satisfies the documented floor in docs/deployment/recommendation.md (MariaDB >= 10.2) and drops two builds. That substitution is REASONING, not something upstream tests. If a migration fails on a collation, fall back to mariadb:10.11 before you debug anything else: the tenant CREATE DATABASE asks for utf8 / utf8_general_ci explicitly (TenantDBManager.ts:64)."

- "REPLACE UPSTREAM'S mariadb BUILD WITH THE OFFICIAL IMAGE PLUS ONE INIT FILE, AND THE INIT FILE IS THE WHOLE TRICK. Write db-init/01-grants.sql containing GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* TO '<your db user>'@'%' WITH GRANT OPTION; followed by FLUSH PRIVILEGES; and mount the directory read-only at /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d. This mirrors docker/mariadb/init.sql upstream. It works because the official entrypoint runs docker_setup_db (which creates MYSQL_DATABASE and MYSQL_USER, and maps MYSQL_* onto MARIADB_*) BEFORE it processes /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d, so the user exists by the time the grant runs. ⚠️ Those files run ONLY on first initialisation of an empty data directory. If you add the grant after the volume already exists it will never run, and the symptom is an organization that builds forever."

1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/bigcapitalhq/bigcapital
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: bigcapitalhq/server:v0.25.31 (plus webapp, envoy, mariadb, redis, gotenberg)
7	  port: 80
8	  vm: m1.large
9	  flavor_id: "4"
10	  database: NONE managed. MariaDB runs inside the compose on the app VM, because Bigcapital creates one database per organization at runtime. Read the second quirk before you plan anything.
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0486
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: bigcapital
16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔⛔ THE SESSION SIGNING KEY IS APP_JWT_SECRET, NOT JWT_SECRET, AND UPSTREAM'S OWN PRODUCTION COMPOSE SETS THE WRONG ONE. packages/server/src/common/config/jwt.ts:4 is process.env.APP_JWT_SECRET with a fallback to a six-character constant that is printed in .env.example, and Auth.module.ts:58-64 hands that value to JwtModule for both signing and verification (HS384). docker-compose.prod.yml:71 passes JWT_SECRET, which no code reads. So a by-the-book upstream deploy signs every session token with a publicly documented constant, and anyone who knows it can mint a valid token for any user on your instance. SET APP_JWT_SECRET to a long random value, and REUSE THE SAME VALUE ON EVERY REDEPLOY: change it and every issued token stops validating and everybody is logged out. Prove it after boot in BOTH directions, because an absence proves nothing: run `sudo docker exec bigcapital-server sh -c 'printenv APP_JWT_SECRET | wc -c'` and confirm the length is far above 7 (this is also what tells you the exec worked at all), then confirm the container is the one serving traffic with `sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Image}}'`. Setting JWT_SECRET as well is harmless and does nothing."
18	  - "⛔⛔ BIGCAPITAL CREATES A NEW DATABASE PER ORGANIZATION AT RUNTIME, SO A redu MANAGED DATABASE CANNOT HOST IT, AND THAT IS WHY THE DATABASE IS IN THE COMPOSE. modules/TenantDBManager/TenantDBManager.ts:60-66 issues CREATE DATABASE <prefix><organizationId> on the SYSTEM connection every time an organization is built (BuildOrganization.service.ts:59-62), and TenantDBManager.ts:86 drops it again. Upstream makes that work with one line in docker/mariadb/init.sql: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* to the app user WITH GRANT OPTION. redu's managed MySQL and MariaDB grant ALL PRIVILEGES on ONE database only, and the superuser flag that managed Postgres honours is not implemented for those engines, so the CREATE DATABASE is refused and the failure lands AFTER the account already exists: you get a user who can sign in and an organization that never finishes building. Managed Postgres is not an alternative either, because system-database.ts:5 and tenant-database.ts:5 both hardcode client: mysql. WHAT THIS FORCES, say it to the user before they approve the plan: your books live on the app VM's own disk, on a docker volume, with no managed database beside them. Nothing else on redu backs that volume up for you, delete_deployment destroys it, and a mysqldump on a schedule is now YOUR job. If you would rather have a managed MariaDB, the only way is to add GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* by hand on the managed DB VM: that works, it costs another GBP 0.0174/hr, and it is NOT durable, because a DB VM rebuild loses the grant and the next organization someone creates fails."
19	  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: NOBODY, UNLESS YOU CLOSE SIGNUP AT DEPLOY TIME. There is no instance-wide admin account and no install wizard. Every signup creates its OWN organization and owns it (AuthSignup.service.ts:66 calls createTenant for each one), and building that organization creates another MySQL database on your VM. Registration is OPEN by default: signup-restrictions.ts:6 defaults SIGNUP_DISABLED to false, and AuthSignup.service.ts:111-112 returns early from the restriction check when it is false, which means SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS and SIGNUP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS are COMPLETELY INERT on their own. The safe-by-construction pattern, and it is a real one here: set SIGNUP_DISABLED=true AND SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS to the operator's own address BEFORE the hostname exists. Only that address can then register, and the first account it creates owns the first organization. Leave the default in place on a public hostname and any stranger can create an account, an organization and a database on your VM, and you are paying for the disk."

43	
44	# Self-host Bigcapital on redu
45	
46	Double-entry accounting and inventory for a small business: invoices, bills, banking, financial
47	reports, on your own EU-hosted VM with a public HTTPS URL and nobody else holding your ledger.
48	
49	## What this deploys
50	
51	- **Bigcapital server and webapp** from the official images, pinned, behind upstream's own envoy
52	  proxy on port 80, which redu fronts with TLS.
53	- **MariaDB and Redis inside the compose**, on volumes on the app VM. Read the next section: this
54	  is the one entry in the library where the database is not managed, and there is a reason.
55	- **Gotenberg** for PDF rendering, on the private compose network only.
56	- One m1.large VM (4 vCPU / 8 GB / 80 GB), about GBP 0.0486 an hour, roughly GBP 35 a month.
57	
58	**Not eligible for the no-card free trial**, which caps the VM at m1.medium.
59	
60	## Deploy
61	
62	Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
63	directory containing this file:
64	
65	    Read redu.md and deploy Bigcapital on redu.
66	
67	The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.
68	
69	## The thing to understand before you approve
70	
71	Bigcapital is multi-tenant by design. **Every organization gets its own MySQL database, created at
72	the moment the organization is built**, and dropped when it is deleted. redu's managed databases
73	are provisioned with rights over exactly one database, which is the correct shape for almost every
74	app and the wrong shape for this one: the create is refused, and the failure arrives after the
75	account already exists.
76	
77	So this recipe runs MariaDB in the compose, on a volume on the app VM. The consequence is worth
78	saying plainly, because it is your accounting data:
79	
80	- Nothing takes a backup for you. A scheduled `mysqldump` is your job from day one.
81	- `delete_deployment` destroys the volume and the books with it.
82	- A managed MariaDB is possible only by adding a global grant by hand on the database VM, which
83	  costs another GBP 0.0174 an hour and does not survive a rebuild of that VM.
84	
85	## The four that actually break it
86	
87	**`S3_BUCKET` is a boot requirement, not an attachments setting.** This is the one that actually
88	bit on the first real deploy. `Attachment.module.js` constructs multer-s3 storage eagerly at
89	module init, and multer-s3 throws `bucket is required` when the bucket is undefined — killing the
90	entire Nest app. The symptom is deceptive: redu reports `ready`, `/` serves the SPA with a 200
91	because that is a different container, and every `/api` path answers 503 while the server
92	restart-loops. Set `S3_BUCKET` to a placeholder even if nobody will ever upload a document.
93	
94	**The signing key has the wrong name in upstream's own compose.** The server reads
95	`APP_JWT_SECRET`; the production compose sets `JWT_SECRET`, which nothing reads, so the
96	fallback constant published in `.env.example` signs every session token. Set
97	`APP_JWT_SECRET` yourself, and set the same value on every redeploy.
98	
99	**Signup is open, and the allow-lists do nothing on their own.** `SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` is
100	ignored entirely unless `SIGNUP_DISABLED=true` is set as well. Set both at deploy time and only
101	your address can register.
102	
103	**The webapp container cannot serve the API.** Its nginx has no `/api` route, so exposing it
104	directly gives you a UI that 404s on everything. Envoy is the ingress.
105	
106	## Prove the signup window is actually shut
107	
108	Run this after the URL answers. It refuses to give an opinion when it cannot tell.
109	
110	```bash
111	#!/usr/bin/env bash
112	# usage: check-signup.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
113	# exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN (act now), 2 = inconclusive (re-run or investigate)
114	set -u
115	HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"
116	
117	# 1. Require a 200 and something Bigcapital-specific in the body. redu's proxy answers 502 for
118	#    roughly the first 2.5 minutes while containers start, and an error page fails every
119	#    assertion below in a way that reads like a pass.
120	resp="$(curl -sS -m 20 -w '\n%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
121	code="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | tail -n1)"
122	body="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | sed '$d')"
123	
124	if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
125	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the proxy, the stack is still starting. Re-run in a minute."
126	  exit 2
127	fi
128	if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
129	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/auth/meta answered $code, not 200. Not talking to Bigcapital."
130	  exit 2
131	fi
132	# v0.25.31 returns snake_case {"signup_disabled":true}. Accept both spellings: grepping only
133	# for signupDisabled reports INCONCLUSIVE against a perfectly healthy instance.
134	case "$body" in
135	  *signup_disabled*|*signupDisabled*) : ;;
136	  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but no signup flag in the body. Wrong service?"; exit 2 ;;
137	esac
138	echo "reported by the app: $body"
139	
140	# 2. Positive control. The signup route must EXIST, or the refusal below means nothing.
141	probe="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' \
142	  -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary '{}' \
143	  "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"
144	case "$probe" in
145	  404|000) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup route answered $probe, so the test below is vacuous."; exit 2 ;;
146	esac
147	echo "signup route is live (empty body answered $probe)"
148	
149	# 3. The behaviour itself, not the flag. Try a real anonymous signup from an address that is not
150	#    on the allow-list. Body on stdin so it never appears in ps.
151	rnd="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'a-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 12)"
152	throwaway="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)"
153	attempt="$(printf '{"firstName":"probe","lastName":"probe","email":"%s@example.invalid","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' \
154	  "$rnd" "$throwaway" |
155	  curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 30 -w '%{http_code}' \
156	    -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
157	    "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"
158	
159	case "$attempt" in
160	  200|201)
161	    echo "FAIL: an anonymous stranger just created an account and an organization ($attempt)."
162	    echo "Set SIGNUP_DISABLED=true and SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS, restart the server, re-run this."
163	    exit 1 ;;
164	  400|401|403|422)
165	    echo "OK: anonymous signup refused ($attempt), and the route was proven live first."
166	    exit 0 ;;
167	  *)
168	    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $attempt from the signup route."
169	    exit 2 ;;
170	esac
171	```
172	
173	## Prove the migration actually ran
174	
175	Both halves. The second command is what makes the first one's number mean anything.
176	
177	```bash
178	#!/usr/bin/env bash
179	# Run on the VM. $DBC is the MariaDB container name from: sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'
180	set -u
181	DBC="${1:?pass the mariadb container name}"
182	
183	# Positive control: the client exists and the server answers. Without this, a "0 tables" answer
184	# below could just be a command that never ran.
185	# ⚠️ The variable INSIDE the container is whatever the compose set, and this recipe sets
186	#    MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD. The official entrypoint maps MYSQL_* onto MARIADB_* for its own setup
187	#    logic; it does NOT export MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD into the container environment, so
188	#    -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" expands to empty and this fails INCONCLUSIVE on a healthy DB.
189	sudo docker exec "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N -e "SELECT 1"' \
190	  || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: cannot reach MariaDB in $DBC at all"; exit 2; }
191	
192	# The system database must hold tables once the system migration has run. SQL on stdin, so there
193	# is no nested quoting to get wrong and nothing lands in ps.
194	sql="SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'bigcapital_system';"
195	n="$(printf '%s\n' "$sql" | sudo docker exec -i "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N')"
196	echo "tables in bigcapital_system: $n"
197	[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "FAIL: the system migration did not run"; exit 1; }
198	echo "OK"
199	```
200	
201	## Prove the API is actually alive, not just the SPA
202	
203	The `S3_BUCKET` crash makes `/` answer 200 while the app is dead, so checking the front page
204	proves nothing. Check an API path and the container state together.
205	
206	```bash
207	#!/usr/bin/env bash
208	# usage: check-api.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
209	set -u
210	HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"
211	root="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/" || true)"
212	api="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
213	echo "/ = $root   /api/auth/meta = $api"
214	if [ "$root" = "200" ] && [ "$api" = "503" ]; then
215	  echo "FAIL: the SPA is up and the server is NOT. Almost always a crash-looping server."
216	  echo "On the VM: sudo docker logs --tail 40 bigcapital-server   (look for 'bucket is required')"
217	  exit 1
218	fi
219	[ "$api" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api answered $api"; exit 2; }
220	echo "OK: the API is serving."
221	```
222	
223	## Deploy log
224	
225	- **2026-08-17, deploy #437: ready** at https://bigcapital-hqw3u9l9.redu.cloud on m1.large,
226	  GBP 0.0486/hr. First real deployment of this recipe; the figures below are now measurements,
227	  not reasoning.
228	  - **7 min 54 s** from `deploy_compose` to `status=ready` (image pulls only; nothing is built).
229	  - **The deploy did not work on the first try.** The server crash-looped on
230	    `Error: bucket is required` because `S3_BUCKET` was unset, while redu reported `ready` and
231	    `/` served the SPA. Fixed by setting a placeholder `S3_BUCKET`; recorded as the top quirk.
232	  - Idle memory 1017 MB / 7941 MB, containers ~326 MiB total; disk 7.3 GB / 77 GB.
233	  - Verified: system migration ran (17 tables in `bigcapital_system`); the global grant applied,
234	    and `CREATE DATABASE ... utf8/utf8_general_ci` succeeds **as the app user** on
235	    mariadb:11.4.12, so the collation fallback to 10.11 was not needed; `APP_JWT_SECRET` is 64
236	    chars inside the running container and `JWT_SECRET` is unset; signup refused for a
237	    non-allow-listed address with `400 SIGNUP_RESTRICTED_NOT_ALLOWED` after proving the route live.
238	  - Two verification scripts in this file were wrong as written and are now fixed: the signup key
239	    is `signup_disabled`, and the MariaDB root password inside the container is
240	    `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`.
241	  - Not verified on this run, because it needs a real account: building an organization
242	    end-to-end (the BullMQ job, the per-tenant `CREATE DATABASE`). The grant and the queue are
243	    both proven present, but the full path has not been exercised.

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/bigcapitalhq/bigcapital
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: bigcapitalhq/server:v0.25.31 (plus webapp, envoy, mariadb, redis, gotenberg)
  port: 80
  vm: m1.large
  flavor_id: "4"
  database: NONE managed. MariaDB runs inside the compose on the app VM, because Bigcapital creates one database per organization at runtime. Read the second quirk before you plan anything.

# Self-host Bigcapital on redu

Double-entry accounting and inventory for a small business: invoices, bills, banking, financial
reports, on your own EU-hosted VM with a public HTTPS URL and nobody else holding your ledger.

## What this deploys

- **Bigcapital server and webapp** from the official images, pinned, behind upstream's own envoy
  proxy on port 80, which redu fronts with TLS.
- **MariaDB and Redis inside the compose**, on volumes on the app VM. Read the next section: this
  is the one entry in the library where the database is not managed, and there is a reason.
- **Gotenberg** for PDF rendering, on the private compose network only.
- One m1.large VM (4 vCPU / 8 GB / 80 GB), about GBP 0.0486 an hour, roughly GBP 35 a month.

**Not eligible for the no-card free trial**, which caps the VM at m1.medium.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Bigcapital on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The thing to understand before you approve

Bigcapital is multi-tenant by design. **Every organization gets its own MySQL database, created at
the moment the organization is built**, and dropped when it is deleted. redu's managed databases
are provisioned with rights over exactly one database, which is the correct shape for almost every
app and the wrong shape for this one: the create is refused, and the failure arrives after the
account already exists.

So this recipe runs MariaDB in the compose, on a volume on the app VM. The consequence is worth
saying plainly, because it is your accounting data:

- Nothing takes a backup for you. A scheduled `mysqldump` is your job from day one.
- `delete_deployment` destroys the volume and the books with it.
- A managed MariaDB is possible only by adding a global grant by hand on the database VM, which
  costs another GBP 0.0174 an hour and does not survive a rebuild of that VM.

## The four that actually break it

**`S3_BUCKET` is a boot requirement, not an attachments setting.** This is the one that actually
bit on the first real deploy. `Attachment.module.js` constructs multer-s3 storage eagerly at
module init, and multer-s3 throws `bucket is required` when the bucket is undefined — killing the
entire Nest app. The symptom is deceptive: redu reports `ready`, `/` serves the SPA with a 200
because that is a different container, and every `/api` path answers 503 while the server
restart-loops. Set `S3_BUCKET` to a placeholder even if nobody will ever upload a document.

**The signing key has the wrong name in upstream's own compose.** The server reads
`APP_JWT_SECRET`; the production compose sets `JWT_SECRET`, which nothing reads, so the
fallback constant published in `.env.example` signs every session token. Set
`APP_JWT_SECRET` yourself, and set the same value on every redeploy.

**Signup is open, and the allow-lists do nothing on their own.** `SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` is
ignored entirely unless `SIGNUP_DISABLED=true` is set as well. Set both at deploy time and only
your address can register.

**The webapp container cannot serve the API.** Its nginx has no `/api` route, so exposing it
directly gives you a UI that 404s on everything. Envoy is the ingress.

## Prove the signup window is actually shut

Run this after the URL answers. It refuses to give an opinion when it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: check-signup.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN (act now), 2 = inconclusive (re-run or investigate)
set -u
HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"

# 1. Require a 200 and something Bigcapital-specific in the body. redu's proxy answers 502 for
#    roughly the first 2.5 minutes while containers start, and an error page fails every
#    assertion below in a way that reads like a pass.
resp="$(curl -sS -m 20 -w '\n%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
code="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | tail -n1)"
body="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | sed '$d')"

if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the proxy, the stack is still starting. Re-run in a minute."
  exit 2
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/auth/meta answered $code, not 200. Not talking to Bigcapital."
  exit 2
fi
# v0.25.31 returns snake_case {"signup_disabled":true}. Accept both spellings: grepping only
# for signupDisabled reports INCONCLUSIVE against a perfectly healthy instance.
case "$body" in
  *signup_disabled*|*signupDisabled*) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but no signup flag in the body. Wrong service?"; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "reported by the app: $body"

# 2. Positive control. The signup route must EXIST, or the refusal below means nothing.
probe="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary '{}' \
  "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"
case "$probe" in
  404|000) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup route answered $probe, so the test below is vacuous."; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "signup route is live (empty body answered $probe)"

# 3. The behaviour itself, not the flag. Try a real anonymous signup from an address that is not
#    on the allow-list. Body on stdin so it never appears in ps.
rnd="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'a-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 12)"
throwaway="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)"
attempt="$(printf '{"firstName":"probe","lastName":"probe","email":"%s@example.invalid","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' \
  "$rnd" "$throwaway" |
  curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 30 -w '%{http_code}' \
    -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
    "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"

case "$attempt" in
  200|201)
    echo "FAIL: an anonymous stranger just created an account and an organization ($attempt)."
    echo "Set SIGNUP_DISABLED=true and SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS, restart the server, re-run this."
    exit 1 ;;
  400|401|403|422)
    echo "OK: anonymous signup refused ($attempt), and the route was proven live first."
    exit 0 ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $attempt from the signup route."
    exit 2 ;;
esac
```

## Prove the migration actually ran

Both halves. The second command is what makes the first one's number mean anything.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run on the VM. $DBC is the MariaDB container name from: sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'
set -u
DBC="${1:?pass the mariadb container name}"

# Positive control: the client exists and the server answers. Without this, a "0 tables" answer
# below could just be a command that never ran.
# ⚠️ The variable INSIDE the container is whatever the compose set, and this recipe sets
#    MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD. The official entrypoint maps MYSQL_* onto MARIADB_* for its own setup
#    logic; it does NOT export MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD into the container environment, so
#    -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" expands to empty and this fails INCONCLUSIVE on a healthy DB.
sudo docker exec "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N -e "SELECT 1"' \
  || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: cannot reach MariaDB in $DBC at all"; exit 2; }

# The system database must hold tables once the system migration has run. SQL on stdin, so there
# is no nested quoting to get wrong and nothing lands in ps.
sql="SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'bigcapital_system';"
n="$(printf '%s\n' "$sql" | sudo docker exec -i "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N')"
echo "tables in bigcapital_system: $n"
[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "FAIL: the system migration did not run"; exit 1; }
echo "OK"
```

## Prove the API is actually alive, not just the SPA

The `S3_BUCKET` crash makes `/` answer 200 while the app is dead, so checking the front page
proves nothing. Check an API path and the container state together.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: check-api.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -u
HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"
root="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/" || true)"
api="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
echo "/ = $root   /api/auth/meta = $api"
if [ "$root" = "200" ] && [ "$api" = "503" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: the SPA is up and the server is NOT. Almost always a crash-looping server."
  echo "On the VM: sudo docker logs --tail 40 bigcapital-server   (look for 'bucket is required')"
  exit 1
fi
[ "$api" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api answered $api"; exit 2; }
echo "OK: the API is serving."
```

# Self-host Bigcapital on redu

Double-entry accounting and inventory for a small business: invoices, bills, banking, financial
reports, on your own EU-hosted VM with a public HTTPS URL and nobody else holding your ledger.

## What this deploys

- **Bigcapital server and webapp** from the official images, pinned, behind upstream's own envoy
  proxy on port 80, which redu fronts with TLS.
- **MariaDB and Redis inside the compose**, on volumes on the app VM. Read the next section: this
  is the one entry in the library where the database is not managed, and there is a reason.
- **Gotenberg** for PDF rendering, on the private compose network only.
- One m1.large VM (4 vCPU / 8 GB / 80 GB), about GBP 0.0486 an hour, roughly GBP 35 a month.

**Not eligible for the no-card free trial**, which caps the VM at m1.medium.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Bigcapital on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The thing to understand before you approve

Bigcapital is multi-tenant by design. **Every organization gets its own MySQL database, created at
the moment the organization is built**, and dropped when it is deleted. redu's managed databases
are provisioned with rights over exactly one database, which is the correct shape for almost every
app and the wrong shape for this one: the create is refused, and the failure arrives after the
account already exists.

So this recipe runs MariaDB in the compose, on a volume on the app VM. The consequence is worth
saying plainly, because it is your accounting data:

- Nothing takes a backup for you. A scheduled `mysqldump` is your job from day one.
- `delete_deployment` destroys the volume and the books with it.
- A managed MariaDB is possible only by adding a global grant by hand on the database VM, which
  costs another GBP 0.0174 an hour and does not survive a rebuild of that VM.

## The four that actually break it

**`S3_BUCKET` is a boot requirement, not an attachments setting.** This is the one that actually
bit on the first real deploy. `Attachment.module.js` constructs multer-s3 storage eagerly at
module init, and multer-s3 throws `bucket is required` when the bucket is undefined — killing the
entire Nest app. The symptom is deceptive: redu reports `ready`, `/` serves the SPA with a 200
because that is a different container, and every `/api` path answers 503 while the server
restart-loops. Set `S3_BUCKET` to a placeholder even if nobody will ever upload a document.

**The signing key has the wrong name in upstream's own compose.** The server reads
`APP_JWT_SECRET`; the production compose sets `JWT_SECRET`, which nothing reads, so the
fallback constant published in `.env.example` signs every session token. Set
`APP_JWT_SECRET` yourself, and set the same value on every redeploy.

**Signup is open, and the allow-lists do nothing on their own.** `SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` is
ignored entirely unless `SIGNUP_DISABLED=true` is set as well. Set both at deploy time and only
your address can register.

**The webapp container cannot serve the API.** Its nginx has no `/api` route, so exposing it
directly gives you a UI that 404s on everything. Envoy is the ingress.

## Prove the signup window is actually shut

Run this after the URL answers. It refuses to give an opinion when it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: check-signup.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN (act now), 2 = inconclusive (re-run or investigate)
set -u
HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"

# 1. Require a 200 and something Bigcapital-specific in the body. redu's proxy answers 502 for
#    roughly the first 2.5 minutes while containers start, and an error page fails every
#    assertion below in a way that reads like a pass.
resp="$(curl -sS -m 20 -w '\n%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
code="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | tail -n1)"
body="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | sed '$d')"

if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the proxy, the stack is still starting. Re-run in a minute."
  exit 2
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/auth/meta answered $code, not 200. Not talking to Bigcapital."
  exit 2
fi
# v0.25.31 returns snake_case {"signup_disabled":true}. Accept both spellings: grepping only
# for signupDisabled reports INCONCLUSIVE against a perfectly healthy instance.
case "$body" in
  *signup_disabled*|*signupDisabled*) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but no signup flag in the body. Wrong service?"; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "reported by the app: $body"

# 2. Positive control. The signup route must EXIST, or the refusal below means nothing.
probe="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary '{}' \
  "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"
case "$probe" in
  404|000) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup route answered $probe, so the test below is vacuous."; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "signup route is live (empty body answered $probe)"

# 3. The behaviour itself, not the flag. Try a real anonymous signup from an address that is not
#    on the allow-list. Body on stdin so it never appears in ps.
rnd="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'a-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 12)"
throwaway="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)"
attempt="$(printf '{"firstName":"probe","lastName":"probe","email":"%s@example.invalid","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' \
  "$rnd" "$throwaway" |
  curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 30 -w '%{http_code}' \
    -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
    "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"

case "$attempt" in
  200|201)
    echo "FAIL: an anonymous stranger just created an account and an organization ($attempt)."
    echo "Set SIGNUP_DISABLED=true and SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS, restart the server, re-run this."
    exit 1 ;;
  400|401|403|422)
    echo "OK: anonymous signup refused ($attempt), and the route was proven live first."
    exit 0 ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $attempt from the signup route."
    exit 2 ;;
esac
```

## Prove the migration actually ran

Both halves. The second command is what makes the first one's number mean anything.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run on the VM. $DBC is the MariaDB container name from: sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'
set -u
DBC="${1:?pass the mariadb container name}"

# Positive control: the client exists and the server answers. Without this, a "0 tables" answer
# below could just be a command that never ran.
# ⚠️ The variable INSIDE the container is whatever the compose set, and this recipe sets
#    MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD. The official entrypoint maps MYSQL_* onto MARIADB_* for its own setup
#    logic; it does NOT export MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD into the container environment, so
#    -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" expands to empty and this fails INCONCLUSIVE on a healthy DB.
sudo docker exec "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N -e "SELECT 1"' \
  || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: cannot reach MariaDB in $DBC at all"; exit 2; }

# The system database must hold tables once the system migration has run. SQL on stdin, so there
# is no nested quoting to get wrong and nothing lands in ps.
sql="SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'bigcapital_system';"
n="$(printf '%s\n' "$sql" | sudo docker exec -i "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N')"
echo "tables in bigcapital_system: $n"
[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "FAIL: the system migration did not run"; exit 1; }
echo "OK"
```

## Prove the API is actually alive, not just the SPA

The `S3_BUCKET` crash makes `/` answer 200 while the app is dead, so checking the front page
proves nothing. Check an API path and the container state together.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: check-api.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -u
HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"
root="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/" || true)"
api="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
echo "/ = $root   /api/auth/meta = $api"
if [ "$root" = "200" ] && [ "$api" = "503" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: the SPA is up and the server is NOT. Almost always a crash-looping server."
  echo "On the VM: sudo docker logs --tail 40 bigcapital-server   (look for 'bucket is required')"
  exit 1
fi
[ "$api" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api answered $api"; exit 2; }
echo "OK: the API is serving."
```

structuredContent.redu_md_markdown:
---
last_deploy:
  id: 437
  date: 2026-08-17
  status: ready
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/bigcapitalhq/bigcapital
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: bigcapitalhq/server:v0.25.31 (plus webapp, envoy, mariadb, redis, gotenberg)
  port: 80
  vm: m1.large
  flavor_id: "4"
  database: NONE managed. MariaDB runs inside the compose on the app VM, because Bigcapital creates one database per organization at runtime. Read the second quirk before you plan anything.
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0486
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: bigcapital
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔⛔ THE SESSION SIGNING KEY IS APP_JWT_SECRET, NOT JWT_SECRET, AND UPSTREAM'S OWN PRODUCTION COMPOSE SETS THE WRONG ONE. packages/server/src/common/config/jwt.ts:4 is process.env.APP_JWT_SECRET with a fallback to a six-character constant that is printed in .env.example, and Auth.module.ts:58-64 hands that value to JwtModule for both signing and verification (HS384). docker-compose.prod.yml:71 passes JWT_SECRET, which no code reads. So a by-the-book upstream deploy signs every session token with a publicly documented constant, and anyone who knows it can mint a valid token for any user on your instance. SET APP_JWT_SECRET to a long random value, and REUSE THE SAME VALUE ON EVERY REDEPLOY: change it and every issued token stops validating and everybody is logged out. Prove it after boot in BOTH directions, because an absence proves nothing: run `sudo docker exec bigcapital-server sh -c 'printenv APP_JWT_SECRET | wc -c'` and confirm the length is far above 7 (this is also what tells you the exec worked at all), then confirm the container is the one serving traffic with `sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Image}}'`. Setting JWT_SECRET as well is harmless and does nothing."
  - "⛔⛔ BIGCAPITAL CREATES A NEW DATABASE PER ORGANIZATION AT RUNTIME, SO A redu MANAGED DATABASE CANNOT HOST IT, AND THAT IS WHY THE DATABASE IS IN THE COMPOSE. modules/TenantDBManager/TenantDBManager.ts:60-66 issues CREATE DATABASE <prefix><organizationId> on the SYSTEM connection every time an organization is built (BuildOrganization.service.ts:59-62), and TenantDBManager.ts:86 drops it again. Upstream makes that work with one line in docker/mariadb/init.sql: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* to the app user WITH GRANT OPTION. redu's managed MySQL and MariaDB grant ALL PRIVILEGES on ONE database only, and the superuser flag that managed Postgres honours is not implemented for those engines, so the CREATE DATABASE is refused and the failure lands AFTER the account already exists: you get a user who can sign in and an organization that never finishes building. Managed Postgres is not an alternative either, because system-database.ts:5 and tenant-database.ts:5 both hardcode client: mysql. WHAT THIS FORCES, say it to the user before they approve the plan: your books live on the app VM's own disk, on a docker volume, with no managed database beside them. Nothing else on redu backs that volume up for you, delete_deployment destroys it, and a mysqldump on a schedule is now YOUR job. If you would rather have a managed MariaDB, the only way is to add GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* by hand on the managed DB VM: that works, it costs another GBP 0.0174/hr, and it is NOT durable, because a DB VM rebuild loses the grant and the next organization someone creates fails."
  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: NOBODY, UNLESS YOU CLOSE SIGNUP AT DEPLOY TIME. There is no instance-wide admin account and no install wizard. Every signup creates its OWN organization and owns it (AuthSignup.service.ts:66 calls createTenant for each one), and building that organization creates another MySQL database on your VM. Registration is OPEN by default: signup-restrictions.ts:6 defaults SIGNUP_DISABLED to false, and AuthSignup.service.ts:111-112 returns early from the restriction check when it is false, which means SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS and SIGNUP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS are COMPLETELY INERT on their own. The safe-by-construction pattern, and it is a real one here: set SIGNUP_DISABLED=true AND SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS to the operator's own address BEFORE the hostname exists. Only that address can then register, and the first account it creates owns the first organization. Leave the default in place on a public hostname and any stranger can create an account, an organization and a database on your VM, and you are paying for the disk."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH, verified in Auth.controller.ts:34-37 where @PublicRoute() sits on the whole /auth controller: POST /api/auth/signin, POST /api/auth/signup, POST /api/auth/signup/verify, POST /api/auth/send_reset_password, POST /api/auth/reset_password/:token and GET /api/auth/meta. Everything else is behind the global JWT guard. GET /api/auth/meta returns the signup flag and is the endpoint the verification script in the body of this file uses, along with an actual refused signup, because a flag reporting the right value is not proof the behaviour changed. ⚠️ MEASURED ON v0.25.31: the JSON key is SNAKE_CASE, {\"signup_disabled\":true}, NOT signupDisabled. An assertion grepping for signupDisabled returns INCONCLUSIVE against a perfectly healthy instance; the script below now accepts both. The refusal itself answers 400 with type SIGNUP_RESTRICTED_NOT_ALLOWED, which is how you tell the restriction fired rather than ordinary body validation."
  - "PIN EVERY IMAGE. Upstream's docker-compose.prod.yml uses the rolling tag for bigcapitalhq/webapp and bigcapitalhq/server, a rolling v1.30 tag for envoyproxy/envoy and the bare major 7 for gotenberg/gotenberg. Registry-checked on 2026-08-17: server and webapp both publish v0.25.31, pushed the same day; the rolling envoy v1.30 tag and v1.30.11 return the SAME manifest digest, and the gotenberg major 7 tag and 7.10.2 likewise, so pinning loses nothing at all. Use bigcapitalhq/server:v0.25.31, bigcapitalhq/webapp:v0.25.31, envoyproxy/envoy:v1.30.11 and gotenberg/gotenberg:7.10.2. Keep gotenberg on the 7 line: that is the major version Bigcapital targets and 8 is a different API. Never write a rolling tag into this stack; server and webapp must move together or the SPA calls endpoints the server does not have."
  - "THE DATA SERVICES ARE FORWARD SUBSTITUTIONS AND YOU SHOULD KNOW WHICH LINES ARE OURS. Upstream BUILDS its own mariadb image FROM mariadb:10.2 (EOL 2022) and its own redis FROM redis:6.2.21. This recipe replaces both with official images, mariadb:11.4.12 and redis:7.4.10-alpine, which satisfies the documented floor in docs/deployment/recommendation.md (MariaDB >= 10.2) and drops two builds. That substitution is REASONING, not something upstream tests. If a migration fails on a collation, fall back to mariadb:10.11 before you debug anything else: the tenant CREATE DATABASE asks for utf8 / utf8_general_ci explicitly (TenantDBManager.ts:64). ✅ MEASURED on deploy #437: no fallback was needed. mariadb:11.4.12 ran the system migration to 17 tables, and CREATE DATABASE <name> DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE utf8_general_ci executed cleanly AS THE APP USER (11.4 still accepts utf8 as an alias for utf8mb3). redis:7.4.10-alpine raised nothing either."
  - "REPLACE UPSTREAM'S mariadb BUILD WITH THE OFFICIAL IMAGE PLUS ONE INIT FILE, AND THE INIT FILE IS THE WHOLE TRICK. Write db-init/01-grants.sql containing GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* TO '<your db user>'@'%' WITH GRANT OPTION; followed by FLUSH PRIVILEGES; and mount the directory read-only at /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d. This mirrors docker/mariadb/init.sql upstream. It works because the official entrypoint runs docker_setup_db (which creates MYSQL_DATABASE and MYSQL_USER, and maps MYSQL_* onto MARIADB_*) BEFORE it processes /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d, so the user exists by the time the grant runs. ⚠️ Those files run ONLY on first initialisation of an empty data directory. If you add the grant after the volume already exists it will never run, and the symptom is an organization that builds forever."
  - "⛔ THE INGRESS IS ENVOY, NOT THE WEBAPP CONTAINER. packages/webapp/nginx/sites/default.conf serves the built SPA and has NO /api location at all, while packages/webapp/src/services/ApiService.tsx calls same-origin /api/<resource>. Expose the webapp directly and you get a UI that loads and then 404s on every request, which reads as a broken app rather than a routing mistake. Ship upstream's docker/envoy/envoy.yaml verbatim, mounted at /etc/envoy/envoy.yaml: it routes prefix /api to server:3000 and prefix / to webapp:80, both plain HTTP. Pass port 80 to deploy_compose and let redu terminate TLS. Drop the 443 mapping from the compose; nothing in this stack serves TLS."
  - "⛔ THE MIGRATION IS A SEPARATE ONE-SHOT CONTAINER AND NOTHING ELSE RUNS IT. The server does NOT migrate at boot. Upstream builds docker/migration/Dockerfile from the server image just to run, from /app/packages/server, node dist/cli.js system:migrate:latest followed by node dist/cli.js tenants:migrate:latest (both command names confirmed in modules/CLI/commands; those are nest-commander SUBCOMMAND names that happen to end in the word latest, not image tags, so do not 'fix' them). Do not build that image: add a one-shot service using the PINNED server image with working_dir /app/packages/server and those two commands, restart: 'no', and give it the same DB_* and SYSTEM_DB_* environment as the server. It has no wait-for-it, so wrap it in a bounded retry (roughly: for i in 1..30, try the system migrate, sleep 5 on failure) rather than depending on depends_on, which only waits for the container to start and not for MariaDB to accept connections. Verify it with the script in the body of this file, which checks the system database has tables AND that the check itself ran."
  - "DATABASE WIRING, AND THE VARIABLE NAME REALLY IS MISSPELLED. The server reads DB_HOST, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD, DB_CHARSET, SYSTEM_DB_NAME and TENANT_DB_NAME_PERFIX. That is PERFIX, not PREFIX, in tenant-database.ts:10; spell it correctly and it silently falls back to the built-in default prefix. SYSTEM_DB_* and TENANT_DB_* each fall back to the matching DB_* (system-database.ts:3-8, tenant-database.ts:3-8), so with one MariaDB you only need the DB_* trio plus SYSTEM_DB_NAME. DB_HOST is the compose service name of the MariaDB container, not localhost. There is no DATABASE_URL in this app, so redu's injected PG* variables are irrelevant here: there is no managed database to inject them from."
  - "REDIS IS NOT OPTIONAL, IT IS WHERE ORGANIZATION BUILDS RUN. The build of a new organization is queued as a BullMQ job (Organization/processors/OrganizationBuild.processor.ts), so with no reachable Redis the signup succeeds and the organization never appears, with nothing in the UI to explain it. Set REDIS_HOST and REDIS_PORT and also QUEUE_HOST and QUEUE_PORT: config/redis.ts and config/queue.ts are two separate blocks that each default to localhost, and setting only one of the pairs is a silent half-configuration. Keep Redis in the compose with a volume on /data; it holds jobs, not records, so losing it costs a queue drain."
  - "⛔⛔⛔ S3_BUCKET MUST BE SET OR THE SERVER DOES NOT BOOT AT ALL. MEASURED ON DEPLOY #437, 2026-08-17, AND THIS CORRECTS THE QUIRK BELOW. dist/modules/Attachments/Attachment.module.js builds the MULTER_MODULE_OPTIONS provider EAGERLY at module init with bucket: configService.get('s3.bucket'), and multer-s3 (index.js:114) throws 'bucket is required' the moment that value is undefined. That is a Nest dependency-resolution failure, so the WHOLE application dies: with restart: on-failure you get an endless restart loop, envoy answers 200 on / (the SPA is a different container and loads fine) and 503 on every /api path, and redu still reports the deploy 'ready' because port 80 answers. It reads exactly like a routing bug and is not one. Only S3_BUCKET does this: config/s3.js defaults S3_REGION to 'US' and the S3Client constructor accepts undefined credentials without complaint. SET S3_BUCKET TO A PLACEHOLDER (e.g. bigcapital-attachments-not-configured) even when the user has no bucket. Verified by reading the compiled module on the image and by the crash log itself."
  - "⛔ ATTACHMENTS NEED AN EXTERNAL S3-COMPATIBLE BUCKET, AND redu DOES NOT PROVIDE ONE. Attachments/S3UploadPipeline.ts:18-27 throws 'S3 configuration error: Missing ...' unless S3_REGION, S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID and S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY are all present, and there is no local-disk fallback. So on this recipe the ledger, the invoices and the reports all work and document upload is the ONE feature that does not. Say that to the user up front rather than letting them find it. If they want it, S3_ENDPOINT plus S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE=true points at any S3-compatible provider, and the credentials are theirs, not ours. ⚠️ Read the quirk ABOVE first: the placeholder S3_BUCKET is not optional even for a user who never uploads a document."
  - "SET BASE_URL TO THE PUBLIC HTTPS URL AND GENERATE THE DNAME YOURSELF. config/app.ts:4 reads BASE_URL and it is what mail links and the payment redirect are built from. It must be known at deploy time, so generate the hostname in the full bigcapital-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form yourself; a bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match what you configured."
  - "LEAVE SIGNUP_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION AT ITS DEFAULT UNLESS MAIL IS ACTUALLY CONFIGURED. config/signup-confirmation.ts:5 defaults it to false. Set it to true with no working MAIL_HOST and the verification mail never arrives, so the account you just created cannot be used and you have locked yourself out of the instance you own. Configure mail first, verify a real message arrives, then turn confirmation on."
  - "DELETE THE COMMERCIAL AND TELEMETRY WIRING FROM THE COMPOSE. docker-compose.prod.yml passes Stripe, Plaid, LemonSqueezy, PostHog and seven NEW_RELIC_* variables through to the server. None of them belong in a self-hosted deploy the user did not ask for. Leave them unset, and leave HOSTED_ON_BIGCAPITAL_CLOUD unset: it is the vendor's own cloud flag. Also note line 90 of that file is a real upstream typo, OPEN_EXCHANGE_RATE_APP_ID- with a hyphen instead of an equals, so exchange rates are not configured by the file you are copying even if you fill the value in."
  - "GOTENBERG LISTENS ON 3000, NOT 9000, AND UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE IS WRONG ABOUT IT. docker-compose.prod.yml declares expose: '9000' for the gotenberg service, but .env.example's own production block sets GOTENBERG_URL=http://gotenberg:3000 and 3000 is the gotenberg 7 default. Expose 3000 and point GOTENBERG_URL at it. Set GOTENBERG_DOCS_URL=http://server:3000/public/, which is an INTERNAL address (the server talking to itself over the compose network), not the public BASE_URL."
  - "THE DEPLOY VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN, SO `sudo docker` IS RIGHT. Measured on deploy #437: podman is not installed on the redu compose VM (`sudo podman` is command-not-found) and `docker compose` v2 drives the stack from /opt/app-src, where redu also writes the project .env (root-owned, 0600) holding the values passed as deploy_compose env. There is NO systemd unit for the stack: it comes back after a reboot purely through the containers' restart policy, so every long-lived service needs restart: on-failure (or always) and the one-shot migration correctly has restart: 'no'. To change env after the fact: edit /opt/app-src/.env, reference it from the compose service, then `cd /opt/app-src && sudo docker compose up -d <service>`."

# Self-host Bigcapital on redu

Double-entry accounting and inventory for a small business: invoices, bills, banking, financial
reports, on your own EU-hosted VM with a public HTTPS URL and nobody else holding your ledger.

## What this deploys

- **Bigcapital server and webapp** from the official images, pinned, behind upstream's own envoy
  proxy on port 80, which redu fronts with TLS.
- **MariaDB and Redis inside the compose**, on volumes on the app VM. Read the next section: this
  is the one entry in the library where the database is not managed, and there is a reason.
- **Gotenberg** for PDF rendering, on the private compose network only.
- One m1.large VM (4 vCPU / 8 GB / 80 GB), about GBP 0.0486 an hour, roughly GBP 35 a month.

**Not eligible for the no-card free trial**, which caps the VM at m1.medium.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Bigcapital on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The thing to understand before you approve

Bigcapital is multi-tenant by design. **Every organization gets its own MySQL database, created at
the moment the organization is built**, and dropped when it is deleted. redu's managed databases
are provisioned with rights over exactly one database, which is the correct shape for almost every
app and the wrong shape for this one: the create is refused, and the failure arrives after the
account already exists.

So this recipe runs MariaDB in the compose, on a volume on the app VM. The consequence is worth
saying plainly, because it is your accounting data:

- Nothing takes a backup for you. A scheduled `mysqldump` is your job from day one.
- `delete_deployment` destroys the volume and the books with it.
- A managed MariaDB is possible only by adding a global grant by hand on the database VM, which
  costs another GBP 0.0174 an hour and does not survive a rebuild of that VM.

## The four that actually break it

**`S3_BUCKET` is a boot requirement, not an attachments setting.** This is the one that actually
bit on the first real deploy. `Attachment.module.js` constructs multer-s3 storage eagerly at
module init, and multer-s3 throws `bucket is required` when the bucket is undefined — killing the
entire Nest app. The symptom is deceptive: redu reports `ready`, `/` serves the SPA with a 200
because that is a different container, and every `/api` path answers 503 while the server
restart-loops. Set `S3_BUCKET` to a placeholder even if nobody will ever upload a document.

**The signing key has the wrong name in upstream's own compose.** The server reads
`APP_JWT_SECRET`; the production compose sets `JWT_SECRET`, which nothing reads, so the
fallback constant published in `.env.example` signs every session token. Set
`APP_JWT_SECRET` yourself, and set the same value on every redeploy.

**Signup is open, and the allow-lists do nothing on their own.** `SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` is
ignored entirely unless `SIGNUP_DISABLED=true` is set as well. Set both at deploy time and only
your address can register.

**The webapp container cannot serve the API.** Its nginx has no `/api` route, so exposing it
directly gives you a UI that 404s on everything. Envoy is the ingress.

## Prove the signup window is actually shut

Run this after the URL answers. It refuses to give an opinion when it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: check-signup.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN (act now), 2 = inconclusive (re-run or investigate)
set -u
HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"

# 1. Require a 200 and something Bigcapital-specific in the body. redu's proxy answers 502 for
#    roughly the first 2.5 minutes while containers start, and an error page fails every
#    assertion below in a way that reads like a pass.
resp="$(curl -sS -m 20 -w '\n%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
code="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | tail -n1)"
body="$(printf '%s' "$resp" | sed '$d')"

if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the proxy, the stack is still starting. Re-run in a minute."
  exit 2
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/auth/meta answered $code, not 200. Not talking to Bigcapital."
  exit 2
fi
# v0.25.31 returns snake_case {"signup_disabled":true}. Accept both spellings: grepping only
# for signupDisabled reports INCONCLUSIVE against a perfectly healthy instance.
case "$body" in
  *signup_disabled*|*signupDisabled*) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but no signup flag in the body. Wrong service?"; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "reported by the app: $body"

# 2. Positive control. The signup route must EXIST, or the refusal below means nothing.
probe="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary '{}' \
  "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"
case "$probe" in
  404|000) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup route answered $probe, so the test below is vacuous."; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "signup route is live (empty body answered $probe)"

# 3. The behaviour itself, not the flag. Try a real anonymous signup from an address that is not
#    on the allow-list. Body on stdin so it never appears in ps.
rnd="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'a-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 12)"
throwaway="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)"
attempt="$(printf '{"firstName":"probe","lastName":"probe","email":"%s@example.invalid","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' \
  "$rnd" "$throwaway" |
  curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 30 -w '%{http_code}' \
    -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
    "https://$HOST/api/auth/signup" || true)"

case "$attempt" in
  200|201)
    echo "FAIL: an anonymous stranger just created an account and an organization ($attempt)."
    echo "Set SIGNUP_DISABLED=true and SIGNUP_ALLOWED_EMAILS, restart the server, re-run this."
    exit 1 ;;
  400|401|403|422)
    echo "OK: anonymous signup refused ($attempt), and the route was proven live first."
    exit 0 ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $attempt from the signup route."
    exit 2 ;;
esac
```

## Prove the migration actually ran

Both halves. The second command is what makes the first one's number mean anything.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run on the VM. $DBC is the MariaDB container name from: sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'
set -u
DBC="${1:?pass the mariadb container name}"

# Positive control: the client exists and the server answers. Without this, a "0 tables" answer
# below could just be a command that never ran.
# ⚠️ The variable INSIDE the container is whatever the compose set, and this recipe sets
#    MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD. The official entrypoint maps MYSQL_* onto MARIADB_* for its own setup
#    logic; it does NOT export MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD into the container environment, so
#    -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" expands to empty and this fails INCONCLUSIVE on a healthy DB.
sudo docker exec "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N -e "SELECT 1"' \
  || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: cannot reach MariaDB in $DBC at all"; exit 2; }

# The system database must hold tables once the system migration has run. SQL on stdin, so there
# is no nested quoting to get wrong and nothing lands in ps.
sql="SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'bigcapital_system';"
n="$(printf '%s\n' "$sql" | sudo docker exec -i "$DBC" sh -c 'mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -N')"
echo "tables in bigcapital_system: $n"
[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "FAIL: the system migration did not run"; exit 1; }
echo "OK"
```

## Prove the API is actually alive, not just the SPA

The `S3_BUCKET` crash makes `/` answer 200 while the app is dead, so checking the front page
proves nothing. Check an API path and the container state together.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: check-api.sh bigcapital-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -u
HOST="${1:?pass the hostname}"
root="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/" || true)"
api="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 20 -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/auth/meta" || true)"
echo "/ = $root   /api/auth/meta = $api"
if [ "$root" = "200" ] && [ "$api" = "503" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: the SPA is up and the server is NOT. Almost always a crash-looping server."
  echo "On the VM: sudo docker logs --tail 40 bigcapital-server   (look for 'bucket is required')"
  exit 1
fi
[ "$api" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api answered $api"; exit 2; }
echo "OK: the API is serving."
```

content.text:
Deployed and verified.

## Bigcapital is live

**https://bigcapital-hqw3u9l9.redu.cloud** — deployment `437`, m1.large, **£0.0486/hr (~£35.48/mo)**, billed hourly.

**It did not work on the first attempt, and the recipe didn't predict why.** redu reported `ready` and the front page served a 200, but every `/api` path answered 503: the server was crash-looping on `Error: bucket is required`. `Attachment.module.js` builds multer-s3 storage *eagerly at module init*, so an unset `S3_BUCKET` kills the entire Nest app — it is a boot requirement, not an attachments setting. redu.md described attachments as merely non-functional without S3. I set a placeholder bucket, and the server came up clean.

### What I verified, not assumed
- **Signup is shut.** `{"signup_disabled":true}`, signup route proven live first, then a real anonymous signup refused with `400 SIGNUP_RESTRICTED_NOT_ALLOWED` — the restriction firing, not incidental validation. A non-public route returns 401.
- **`APP_JWT_SECRET`** is 64 random chars inside the running container (not the six-character published constant); `JWT_SECRET` is unset, as it should be.
- **Migration ran** — 17 tables in `bigcapital_system`, with a positive control proving the check itself executed.
- **The per-organization grant works** — `CREATE DATABASE … utf8/utf8_general_ci` succeeds *as the app user*. MariaDB 11.4.12 needed no fallback to 10.11.
- **Measured:** ready in 7m54s; idle 1017 MB / 7941 MB RAM, ~326 MiB across containers; 7.3 GB / 77 GB disk.

Not exercised: building an organization end-to-end. That needs a real account, and the account is yours to create.

### Your next step — claim ownership
Register at the URL with **«REDACTED:env:013044ef»**. It's the only address that can, and the first account it creates owns the first organization. Nobody is an administrator until you do this.

### Credentials — save these now, they're not written to any file
```
APP_JWT_SECRET   «REDACTED:entropy:467a57e4»
DB_PASSWORD      «REDACTED:entropy:30927f0d»
DB_ROOT_PASSWORD «REDACTED:entropy:1cbbf243»
```
Reuse `APP_JWT_SECRET` on every redeploy — changing it logs everyone out permanently.

### Three standing facts
- **Backups are yours from today.** Your ledger sits on a docker volume on that one VM. Nothing on redu backs it up, and `delete_deployment` destroys the books with it. A scheduled `mysqldump` of `bigcapital_system` *and* every `bigcapital_tenant_*` database is now your job.
- **Document upload will not work** until you supply a real S3-compatible bucket and credentials. Everything else — invoices, bills, banking, reports — works.
- The VM runs **docker**, not podman, from `/opt/app-src`. SSH: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/redu-deploy-test -p 22004 ubuntu@bigcapital-hqw3u9l9.redu.cloud`.

### Files written
- `redu.md` — merged by redu, plus five hand-added quirks this run earned (the `S3_BUCKET` boot crash, the `signup_disabled` key name, gotenberg on 3000, docker-not-podman, and the real memory/timing numbers). **Two verification scripts in it were wrong as written** and are now fixed: they'd have reported INCONCLUSIVE against this healthy instance.
- `redu-deploy-plan.md` — replaced with the real deployed values.
- `deploy/` — the exact compose, envoy config, grants file, and signup checker, with the `S3_BUCKET` fix included so a redeploy carries it. I applied that fix live on the VM; the tarball already uploaded to redu is the pre-fix one, so redeploy from `deploy/` rather than reusing that source.

You don't have one yet — and that's expected, not an oversight.

**There is no Bigcapital account password.** No account exists on the instance. Bigcapital has no install wizard and no seeded admin: you create the first account yourself by registering at https://bigcapital-hqw3u9l9.redu.cloud with **«REDACTED:env:013044ef»**, and **you choose the password at that moment**. That account then owns the first organization. Nobody else can register — signup is closed to every other address.

The three values I generated are infrastructure secrets, not login credentials. Repeating them here so they're in one place:

```
APP_JWT_SECRET     «REDACTED:entropy:467a57e4»
DB_PASSWORD        «REDACTED:entropy:30927f0d»   (MariaDB app user 'bigcapital')
DB_ROOT_PASSWORD   «REDACTED:entropy:1cbbf243»   (MariaDB root)
```

None of those will log you into the web UI. Save them anyway — `APP_JWT_SECRET` must be identical on every redeploy or every session token stops validating, and the DB passwords are what you'll need for `mysqldump` backups.

One thing worth knowing before you register: email confirmation is off (deliberately — no mail server is configured), so your account is usable the instant you create it. Don't turn `SIGNUP_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION` on until mail actually works, or the confirmation link never arrives and you lock yourself out of your own instance.
